note: 'Baju hangat' literally means 'warm clothes/shirt' and is the common everyday term for a sweater or jacket; sometimes interchangeable with 'jaket' for light jackets.

sentences.text: Aku pakai baju hangat karena dingin.
sentences.en: I wear a sweater because it is cold.

sentences.text: Di Bali, baju hangat jarang dipakai.
sentences.en: In Bali, sweaters are rarely worn.

sentences.text: Dia membeli baju hangat baru kemarin.
sentences.en: She bought a new sweater yesterday.

note: 'Baju tidur' literally means 'sleep clothes'; often interchangeable with 'piyama', and more commonly used in everyday Indonesian speech than the borrowed word.

sentences.text: Saya memakai baju tidur yang nyaman.
sentences.en: I am wearing comfortable pajamas.

sentences.text: Dia membeli baju tidur baru kemarin.
sentences.en: She bought new pajamas yesterday.

sentences.text: Baju tidur saya ada di kamar.
sentences.en: My pajamas are in the bedroom.

note: 'Blus' is the standard Indonesian word for blouse; it is a loanword from Dutch, used in everyday and formal contexts, related to 'kemeja' (shirt) and 'baju' (clothing/top).

sentences.text: Ibu membeli blus baru di pasar.
sentences.en: Mom bought a new blouse at the market.

sentences.text: Blus merah itu sangat cantik.
sentences.en: That red blouse is very pretty.

sentences.text: Saya suka blus biru ini.
sentences.en: I like this blue blouse.

note: 'Buatan' means 'made in' or 'made by'; often used before a country or person, e.g. 'buatan Indonesia'; related to 'buat' (to make).

sentences.text: Sepatu ini buatan Indonesia.
sentences.en: These shoes are made in Indonesia.

sentences.text: Kue ini buatan ibu saya.
sentences.en: This cake is made by my mother.

sentences.text: Tas itu buatan Bali.
sentences.en: That bag is made in Bali.

note: 'Celana' means pants/trousers; say 'celana pendek' for shorts and 'celana panjang' for long pants; commonly used in everyday shopping and clothing talk.

sentences.text: Saya membeli celana baru di pasar.
sentences.en: I bought new pants at the market.

sentences.text: Celana ini terlalu besar untuk saya.
sentences.en: These pants are too big for me.

sentences.text: Dia memakai celana pendek berwarna biru.
sentences.en: He is wearing blue shorts.

note: 'Celana dalam' is the neutral everyday term for underpants/underwear; it is not vulgar but is considered a private topic, so use it matter-of-factly in practical contexts like shopping or laundry.

sentences.text: Saya membeli celana dalam di toko.
sentences.en: I buy underpants at the store.

sentences.text: Celana dalam saya ada di lemari.
sentences.en: My underpants are in the wardrobe.

sentences.text: Dia mencuci celana dalam setiap hari.
sentences.en: She washes her underpants every day.

note: "Celana pendek" literally means "short pants"; use "celana panjang" for long pants; common casual/everyday clothing word.

sentences.text: Saya memakai celana pendek di pantai.
sentences.en: I am wearing shorts at the beach.

sentences.text: Dia membeli celana pendek baru kemarin.
sentences.en: He bought new shorts yesterday.

sentences.text: Celana pendek ini sangat nyaman.
sentences.en: These shorts are very comfortable.

note: 'Cucian' means laundry (clothes to be washed or already washed); related to 'cuci' (to wash); common in everyday household talk.

sentences.text: Cucian saya belum kering hari ini.
sentences.en: My laundry is not dry yet today.

sentences.text: Ibu mencuci cucian di belakang rumah.
sentences.en: Mom washes the laundry behind the house.

sentences.text: Tolong taruh cucian di keranjang itu.
sentences.en: Please put the laundry in that basket.

note: 'Dasi' means necktie; commonly worn in formal or office settings in Indonesia; related word: 'kemeja' (dress shirt).

sentences.text: Ayah memakai dasi merah ke kantor.
sentences.en: Father wears a red necktie to the office.

sentences.text: Dasi ini bagus sekali.
sentences.en: This necktie is very nice.

sentences.text: Saya beli dasi baru kemarin.
sentences.en: I bought a new necktie yesterday.

note: 'Jaket' means jacket or light coat; more common than 'mantel' (heavy coat); used for hoodies and zip-ups too.

sentences.text: Saya memakai jaket karena cuaca dingin.
sentences.en: I am wearing a jacket because the weather is cold.

sentences.text: Jaket merah itu milik Budi.
sentences.en: That red jacket belongs to Budi.

sentences.text: Dia membeli jaket baru di pasar.
sentences.en: She bought a new jacket at the market.

note: 'Kaus' means t-shirt; also spelled 'kaos'; not to be confused with 'kaus kaki' (socks).

sentences.text: Saya membeli kaus baru di pasar.
sentences.en: I bought a new t-shirt at the market.

sentences.text: Kaus ini berwarna merah dan murah.
sentences.en: This t-shirt is red and cheap.

sentences.text: Dia memakai kaus putih setiap hari.
sentences.en: He wears a white t-shirt every day.

note: 'Kemeja' refers specifically to a collared button-up shirt; often confused with 'baju' (generic top/shirt) or 'kaos' (T-shirt).

sentences.text: Dia memakai kemeja putih ke kantor.
sentences.en: He wears a white shirt to the office.

sentences.text: Saya beli kemeja baru di pasar.
sentences.en: I bought a new shirt at the market.

sentences.text: Kemeja ini sangat bagus dan murah.
sentences.en: This shirt is very nice and cheap.

note: 'Lengan' means both 'arm' (body part) and 'sleeve' (of clothing); beginners often confuse it with 'tangan' which refers to the hand or entire arm casually.

sentences.text: Lengan saya sakit setelah jatuh kemarin.
sentences.en: My arm hurts after falling yesterday.

sentences.text: Baju ini punya lengan yang panjang.
sentences.en: This shirt has long sleeves.

sentences.text: Dia memegang tas di lengan kirinya.
sentences.en: She is holding a bag on her left arm.

note: 'Rok' means skirt; commonly used in everyday clothing talk; related words include 'baju' (shirt) and 'celana' (pants).

sentences.text: Saya memakai rok biru hari ini.
sentences.en: I am wearing a blue skirt today.

sentences.text: Ibu membeli rok baru di pasar.
sentences.en: Mom bought a new skirt at the market.

sentences.text: Rok adik sangat cantik dan panjang.
sentences.en: My younger sister's skirt is very beautiful and long.

note: "Sapu tangan" literally means "hand broom"; it refers to a cloth handkerchief, not a tissue ("tisu"); commonly used in formal or traditional contexts.

sentences.text: Ibu memberi saya sapu tangan baru.
sentences.en: Mother gave me a new handkerchief.

sentences.text: Saya pakai sapu tangan untuk lap muka.
sentences.en: I use a handkerchief to wipe my face.

sentences.text: Di mana sapu tangan saya?
sentences.en: Where is my handkerchief?

note: 'Sedang' has two meanings: 'medium/middle (size)' and 'currently doing something'; context usually clarifies, but pair it with size words to avoid confusion.

sentences.text: Saya mau beli baju ukuran sedang.
sentences.en: I want to buy a shirt in medium size.

sentences.text: Tolong ambilkan tas sedang itu.
sentences.en: Please hand me that medium bag.

sentences.text: Ukuran sedang pas untuk saya.
sentences.en: Medium size fits me well.

note: 'Topi' means hat or cap; common in everyday speech; related: 'topi pantai' (sun hat), 'topi baseball' (baseball cap).

sentences.text: Saya memakai topi di pantai.
sentences.en: I wear a hat at the beach.

sentences.text: Topi merah itu milik Budi.
sentences.en: That red hat belongs to Budi.

sentences.text: Dia membeli topi baru kemarin.
sentences.en: She bought a new hat yesterday.

note: "Ukuran" means both 'size' (e.g. clothing) and 'measurement'; commonly used in shopping and cooking contexts; related words: 'besar' (big), 'kecil' (small), 'mengukur' (to measure).

sentences.text: Berapa ukuran baju kamu?
sentences.en: What is your shirt size?

sentences.text: Ukuran sepatunya terlalu kecil.
sentences.en: The shoe size is too small.

sentences.text: Saya tidak tahu ukuran meja ini.
sentences.en: I don't know the measurement of this table.

note: "Agar" means "in order to / so that"; similar to "supaya" (interchangeable in most casual speech); slightly more formal than "supaya".

sentences.text: Dia belajar keras agar lulus ujian.
sentences.en: He studies hard in order to pass the exam.

sentences.text: Minum air banyak agar tidak sakit.
sentences.en: Drink a lot of water so that you don't get sick.

sentences.text: Saya bangun pagi agar tidak terlambat.
sentences.en: I wake up early in order to not be late.

note: 'Helm' is the everyday Indonesian word for helmet; commonly used for motorcycle helmets since motorbikes are very common in Indonesia.

sentences.text: Kamu harus pakai helm saat naik motor.
sentences.en: You must wear a helmet when riding a motorbike.

sentences.text: Helm saya warnanya merah.
sentences.en: My helmet is red.

sentences.text: Dia lupa membawa helm hari ini.
sentences.en: He forgot to bring a helmet today.

note: 'Ingat' means 'to remember' or 'to recall'; commonly used in daily speech; related words: 'mengingat' (to remember something), 'mengingatkan' (to remind someone)

sentences.text: Aku ingat nama teman baruku.
sentences.en: I remember my new friend's name.

sentences.text: Dia tidak ingat di mana tasnya.
sentences.en: He doesn't remember where his bag is.

sentences.text: Ingat, kita harus pulang sekarang.
sentences.en: Remember, we have to go home now.

english: to give it a good long thought
note: "Diingat-ingat" is a colloquial reduplication meaning to think carefully or recall something thoroughly; commonly used in everyday speech as a gentle reminder.

sentences.text: Tolong diingat-ingat alamat rumah saya ya.
sentences.en: Please give it a good long thought about my home address.

sentences.text: Kata ibu harus diingat-ingat baik-baik.
sentences.en: Mother's words should be given a good long thought.

sentences.text: Jadwal belajar kita perlu diingat-ingat lagi.
sentences.en: Our study schedule needs to be given a good long thought again.

note: 'Jas' refers specifically to a suit jacket or blazer; not to be confused with 'jaket' (casual jacket) or 'baju' (shirt/top).

sentences.text: Dia memakai jas biru ke kantor.
sentences.en: He wears a blue suit jacket to the office.

sentences.text: Jas ini sangat bagus dan mahal.
sentences.en: This suit jacket is very nice and expensive.

sentences.text: Ayah membeli jas baru kemarin.
sentences.en: Dad bought a new suit jacket yesterday.

english: derived from bukan to show a knowledge or understanding shared by speaker and listener
note: "Kan" is an informal tag word (like "right?" or "isn't it?") used to confirm shared knowledge; it comes from "bukan" and is common in casual speech.

sentences.text: Ini kopi, kan?
sentences.en: This is coffee, right?

sentences.text: Kamu tinggal di Bali, kan?
sentences.en: You live in Bali, right?

sentences.text: Besok libur, kan?
sentences.en: Tomorrow is a holiday, right?

note: 'kau' means 'you' and is informal/casual, similar to 'kamu'; avoid in formal situations; related words: 'Anda' (formal), 'kamu' (informal)

sentences.text: Kau mau makan apa malam ini?
sentences.en: What do you want to eat tonight?

sentences.text: Di mana kau tinggal sekarang?
sentences.en: Where do you live now?

sentences.text: Kau sangat baik hati.
sentences.en: You are very kind.

note: 'kelupaan' means to have forgotten something accidentally; informal/colloquial register, related to 'lupa' (forget), often used in everyday speech

sentences.text: Saya kelupaan membawa dompet ke pasar.
sentences.en: I forgot to bring my wallet to the market.

sentences.text: Dia kelupaan nama teman barunya.
sentences.en: She forgot her new friend's name.

sentences.text: Kami kelupaan memesan nasi di warung.
sentences.en: We forgot to order rice at the food stall.

note: 'Kurang' means lacking/not enough; also used before adjectives to mean 'not very' (e.g. kurang baik = not very good); related: kekurangan (shortage).

sentences.text: Nasi ini kurang garam.
sentences.en: This rice lacks salt.

sentences.text: Saya kurang tidur semalam.
sentences.en: I didn't sleep enough last night.

sentences.text: Uang saya kurang untuk beli buku.
sentences.en: My money is not enough to buy a book.

note: "Rasanya" literally means "its taste/feeling" but commonly means "it seems to me" or "I feel like"; don't confuse with "rasa" (taste/feeling) alone; related: "sepertinya" (it seems).

sentences.text: Rasanya hari ini akan hujan.
sentences.en: It seems to me it will rain today.

sentences.text: Rasanya saya sudah pernah ke sini.
sentences.en: It seems to me I have been here before.

sentences.text: Rasanya dia tidak datang hari ini.
sentences.en: It seems to me he is not coming today.

note: "Resmi" means formal or official; often confused with "formal" (borrowed word); related: "resmi" vs. "santai" (casual).

sentences.text: Pertemuan ini bersifat resmi dan penting.
sentences.en: This meeting is formal and important.

sentences.text: Dia memakai baju resmi ke kantor.
sentences.en: He wears formal clothes to the office.

sentences.text: Acara resmi itu mulai jam tujuh.
sentences.en: The formal event starts at seven o'clock.

note: 'SIM' stands for 'Surat Izin Mengemudi'; always use the acronym in everyday speech, never the full form.

sentences.text: Saya perlu membuat SIM bulan ini.
sentences.en: I need to make a driver's license this month.

sentences.text: Apakah kamu sudah punya SIM?
sentences.en: Do you already have a driver's license?

sentences.text: Polisi meminta SIM saya di jalan.
sentences.en: The police asked for my driver's license on the road.

note: "Surat Izin Mengemudi" is the formal term for driver's license, commonly abbreviated as "SIM"; always carry it while driving in Indonesia.

sentences.text: Saya harus membuat Surat Izin Mengemudi baru.
sentences.en: I have to make a new driver's license.

sentences.text: Surat Izin Mengemudi saya ada di dompet.
sentences.en: My driver's license is in my wallet.

sentences.text: Polisi meminta Surat Izin Mengemudi saya.
sentences.en: The police asked for my driver's license.

note: "Siap-siap" is casual/colloquial reduplication of "siap" (ready); more informal than "bersiap"; commonly used in everyday speech to mean "get ready" or "prepare yourself".

sentences.text: Ayo siap-siap, kita pergi ke pantai!
sentences.en: Come on, get ready, we're going to the beach!

sentences.text: Dia siap-siap sebelum pergi ke sekolah.
sentences.en: She gets ready before going to school.

sentences.text: Saya siap-siap untuk makan malam.
sentences.en: I am getting ready for dinner.

english: each and everything, the whole kit and kaboodle
note: 'Segala' means 'all kinds of' or 'everything'; more emphatic than 'semua', often used before nouns to mean 'all sorts of things'.

sentences.text: Warung itu menjual segala jenis makanan.
sentences.en: That small restaurant sells all kinds of food.

sentences.text: Dia tahu segala hal tentang Bali.
sentences.en: She knows everything about Bali.

sentences.text: Pasar ini ada segala kebutuhan dapur.
sentences.en: This market has all kinds of kitchen needs.

note: 'Sementara' means 'while' (simultaneous actions); don't confuse with 'selama' (during a duration) or 'sedangkan' (whereas/contrast).

sentences.text: Saya makan sementara dia menonton TV.
sentences.en: I eat while he watches TV.

sentences.text: Ibu memasak sementara ayah membaca buku.
sentences.en: Mom cooks while Dad reads a book.

sentences.text: Anak-anak bermain sementara saya bekerja.
sentences.en: The children play while I work.

note: Often abbreviated as STNK; required document when driving any vehicle in Indonesia.

sentences.text: Saya butuh Surat Tanda Nomor Kendaraan saya.
sentences.en: I need my motor vehicle registration certificate.

sentences.text: Di mana Surat Tanda Nomor Kendaraan kamu?
sentences.en: Where is your motor vehicle registration certificate?

sentences.text: Polisi minta Surat Tanda Nomor Kendaraan saya.
sentences.en: The police asked for my motor vehicle registration certificate.

note: 'STNK' stands for 'Surat Tanda Nomor Kendaraan'; always carry it when riding a motorbike or driving, as police may check it at roadblocks.

sentences.text: Polisi meminta STNK saya di jalan.
sentences.en: The police asked for my vehicle registration on the road.

sentences.text: Jangan lupa bawa STNK setiap hari.
sentences.en: Don't forget to bring your vehicle registration every day.

sentences.text: Di mana STNK motor kamu?
sentences.en: Where is your motorbike registration certificate?

note: 'Telat' is informal/colloquial for 'terlambat' (late/overdue); very common in everyday speech but avoid in formal writing.

sentences.text: Saya telat ke sekolah hari ini.
sentences.en: I am late to school today.

sentences.text: Bus itu telat dua jam.
sentences.en: That bus is two hours late.

sentences.text: Jangan telat makan obatnya ya.
sentences.en: Don't be late taking your medicine, okay.

note: "Ikat kepala" refers to a traditional head cloth or headband worn in Bali and across Indonesia, especially in ceremonies; also called "udeng" in Balinese context.

sentences.text: Ayah memakai ikat kepala saat upacara.
sentences.en: Father wears a head cloth during the ceremony.

sentences.text: Ikat kepala ini berwarna kuning dan putih.
sentences.en: This head cloth is yellow and white.

sentences.text: Saya membeli ikat kepala di pasar.
sentences.en: I bought a head cloth at the market.

note: Everyday Indonesian word for a headscarf/hijab; commonly used in casual and formal speech; related words: kerudung (similar headscarf), hijab (also widely used).

sentences.text: Ibu membeli jilbab baru di pasar.
sentences.en: Mom bought a new hijab at the market.

sentences.text: Adik memakai jilbab warna merah hari ini.
sentences.en: My younger sister is wearing a red hijab today.

english: a piece of cloth, textile, garment
note: 'Kain' refers to cloth or fabric generally; in Bali it also means the wraparound cloth worn at temples; related words: 'kain batik' (batik cloth), 'kain sarung' (sarong).

sentences.text: Ibu membeli kain batik di pasar.
sentences.en: Mother buys batik cloth at the market.

sentences.text: Kain ini berwarna merah dan putih.
sentences.en: This cloth is red and white.

sentences.text: Saya pakai kain untuk masuk pura.
sentences.en: I wear a cloth to enter the temple.

english: a mostly transparent traditional women blouse
note: 'Kebaya' is a formal traditional blouse worn by women, often at ceremonies or weddings; commonly paired with a 'sarung' or 'kain batik'.

sentences.text: Ibu memakai kebaya merah ke pesta.
sentences.en: Mom wears a red kebaya to the party.

sentences.text: Kebaya ini sangat cantik dan indah.
sentences.en: This kebaya is very pretty and beautiful.

sentences.text: Saya membeli kebaya baru di pasar.
sentences.en: I bought a new kebaya at the market.

note: "Peragaan busana" is the formal/standard term for a fashion show; in casual speech Indonesians also say "fashion show" directly using the English loanword.

sentences.text: Kami menonton peragaan busana di mall.
sentences.en: We watched a fashion show at the mall.

sentences.text: Peragaan busana itu sangat menarik.
sentences.en: The fashion show was very interesting.

sentences.text: Dia ikut peragaan busana kemarin.
sentences.en: She participated in a fashion show yesterday.

note: 'Sarung' is a casual everyday word for the wraparound cloth worn by men at temples or at home; also called 'kain sarung'; do not confuse with 'selendang' (a shawl).

sentences.text: Ayah memakai sarung di rumah.
sentences.en: Father wears a sarong at home.

sentences.text: Saya beli sarung baru kemarin.
sentences.en: I bought a new sarong yesterday.

sentences.text: Sarung ini warnanya bagus sekali.
sentences.en: This sarong has a very nice color.

note: 'Abu-abu' means grey; it is a reduplication of 'abu' (ash), a common pattern for colors in Indonesian; not to be confused with 'abu' alone which just means ash.

sentences.text: Kucing itu berbulu abu-abu dan lucu.
sentences.en: That cat has grey fur and is cute.

sentences.text: Langit hari ini berwarna abu-abu.
sentences.en: The sky today is grey.

sentences.text: Saya punya kaos abu-abu baru.
sentences.en: I have a new grey T-shirt.

note: 'Berpendapat' means to express an opinion or think; more formal than 'pikir', often used in discussions or school contexts.

sentences.text: Saya berpendapat bahwa makanan ini enak.
sentences.en: I think that this food is delicious.

sentences.text: Dia berpendapat kelas hari ini mudah.
sentences.en: She thinks today's class is easy.

sentences.text: Kami berpendapat pasar itu sangat ramai.
sentences.en: We think that market is very crowded.

note: "Dibungkus" is the passive form of "bungkus" (to wrap); commonly used when ordering takeaway food — say "dibungkus" to mean "wrapped to go" instead of eating in.

sentences.text: Nasi goreng ini mau dibungkus, ya?
sentences.en: This fried rice is to be wrapped, right?

sentences.text: Hadiah ulang tahun itu dibungkus kertas merah.
sentences.en: The birthday gift is wrapped in red paper.

sentences.text: Ayam gorengnya dibungkus untuk dibawa pulang.
sentences.en: The fried chicken is wrapped to be taken home.

note: 'Kelihatannya' means 'it seems' or 'it looks like'; it is informal and common in spoken Indonesian, similar to 'sepertinya' but based on the root 'lihat' (to see).

sentences.text: Kelihatannya hari ini akan hujan.
sentences.en: It seems like it will rain today.

sentences.text: Kelihatannya dia sudah makan.
sentences.en: It seems like he has already eaten.

sentences.text: Kelihatannya warung itu tutup sekarang.
sentences.en: It seems like that food stall is closed now.

note: 'Lebar' means wide/broad and also refers to width as a dimension; don't confuse with 'besar' (big/large overall) — 'lebar' is specifically about horizontal span.

sentences.text: Jalan di Bali sangat lebar.
sentences.en: The road in Bali is very wide.

sentences.text: Pantai ini lebar dan indah.
sentences.en: This beach is wide and beautiful.

sentences.text: Berapa lebar meja ini?
sentences.en: How wide is this table?

note: 'Menjahit' is the formal/active form; 'jahit' is the root used in casual speech and compounds like 'tukang jahit' (tailor).

sentences.text: Ibu saya suka menjahit baju di rumah.
sentences.en: My mother likes to sew clothes at home.

sentences.text: Saya belajar menjahit setiap hari Sabtu.
sentences.en: I learn to sew every Saturday.

sentences.text: Nenek menjahit baju baru untuk saya.
sentences.en: Grandma sews a new dress for me.

note: "Pas" means 'to fit' or 'just right'; also used for 'exact change' in shops; related to "cocok" (suitable/matching).

sentences.text: Sepatu ini pas di kaki saya.
sentences.en: These shoes fit my feet.

sentences.text: Baju itu tidak pas untukku.
sentences.en: That shirt does not fit me.

sentences.text: Ukuran cincin ini pas sekali.
sentences.en: The size of this ring fits perfectly.

note: 'Berlatih' means 'to practice' a skill; related to 'latihan' (practice/exercise); commonly used for sports, music, and language learning.

sentences.text: Saya berlatih bahasa Indonesia setiap hari.
sentences.en: I practice Indonesian every day.

sentences.text: Dia berlatih menari di Bali.
sentences.en: She practices dancing in Bali.

sentences.text: Kami berlatih sepak bola bersama.
sentences.en: We practice soccer together.

english: undergarment worn by women to support their breasts
note: "BH" (from Dutch 'bustehouder') is the standard everyday term for bra in Indonesian; very common and not considered vulgar.

sentences.text: Ibu membeli BH baru di pasar.
sentences.en: Mom bought a new bra at the market.

sentences.text: BH ini warnanya putih.
sentences.en: This bra is white in color.

sentences.text: Dia mencuci BH setiap hari.
sentences.en: She washes her bra every day.

note: "Catatan kuliah" means lecture notes at university; "catatan" alone means notes/memo, and "kuliah" means university lecture — avoid confusing with "catatan sekolah" (school notes) for K-12 context.

sentences.text: Saya lupa membawa catatan kuliah hari ini.
sentences.en: I forgot to bring my lecture notes today.

sentences.text: Catatan kuliah saya ada di meja.
sentences.en: My lecture notes are on the table.

sentences.text: Boleh saya pinjam catatan kuliah kamu?
sentences.en: May I borrow your lecture notes?

note: 'Cek' is used in everyday Indonesian for a bank cheque; not to be confused with 'cek' meaning 'to check' — context makes the difference; related: 'uang' (money), 'bank'.

sentences.text: Dia membayar dengan cek di bank.
sentences.en: He pays with a cheque at the bank.

sentences.text: Saya menulis cek untuk membayar sewa.
sentences.en: I write a cheque to pay the rent.

sentences.text: Cek itu dari bank besar.
sentences.en: That cheque is from a big bank.

note: 'Deterjen' is the everyday Indonesian word for laundry or dish detergent; it is a loanword and commonly used in both formal and informal registers.

sentences.text: Ibu membeli deterjen di warung.
sentences.en: Mom buys detergent at the small shop.

sentences.text: Saya pakai deterjen untuk cuci baju.
sentences.en: I use detergent to wash clothes.

sentences.text: Deterjen ini wangi sekali.
sentences.en: This detergent smells very nice.

note: 'Dibuang' is the passive form of 'buang' (to throw away); often confused with 'membuang' (active form); related: 'tempat sampah' (trash can).

sentences.text: Sampah itu harus dibuang ke tempat sampah.
sentences.en: That trash must be thrown away into the trash can.

sentences.text: Makanan lama ini sudah dibuang.
sentences.en: This old food has already been thrown away.

sentences.text: Botol plastik itu dibuang oleh Budi.
sentences.en: That plastic bottle was thrown away by Budi.

note: "Dijahit" is the passive form of "jahit" (to sew); used when something is being sewn by someone, common in everyday clothing repair contexts.

sentences.text: Bajuku dijahit oleh ibu tadi.
sentences.en: My shirt was sewn by mom just now.

sentences.text: Celana ini perlu dijahit lagi.
sentences.en: These pants need to be sewn again.

note: 'Dipegang' is the passive form of 'pegang' (to hold); used when something is being held by someone, common in everyday speech.

sentences.text: Buku itu dipegang oleh anak kecil.
sentences.en: That book is held by a small child.

sentences.text: Balon merah dipegang ibu di pasar.
sentences.en: The red balloon is held by mom at the market.

sentences.text: Tas itu dipegang dengan kuat.
sentences.en: That bag is held tightly.

note: 'Dipinjam' is the passive form of 'pinjam' (to borrow); use it when something is being borrowed by someone, common confusion is mixing it with 'meminjam' (active: to borrow) vs 'dipinjam' (passive: to be borrowed).

sentences.text: Buku ini sedang dipinjam oleh Ari.
sentences.en: This book is being borrowed by Ari.

sentences.text: Sepeda saya dipinjam teman kemarin.
sentences.en: My bicycle was borrowed by a friend yesterday.

sentences.text: Pensil itu sudah dipinjam kakak.
sentences.en: That pencil has already been borrowed by my older sibling.

note: "Dipotong" is the passive form of "potong" (to cut); commonly used for hair, nails, prices, or connections being cut.

sentences.text: Rambut saya dipotong di salon hari ini.
sentences.en: My hair is being cut at the salon today.

sentences.text: Harga itu dipotong menjadi lebih murah.
sentences.en: That price was cut to be cheaper.

sentences.text: Listrik di rumah dipotong tadi malam.
sentences.en: The electricity at home was cut off last night.

note: 'Diseterika' is the passive form of 'seterika' (to iron); used when clothes are the subject being ironed, common in everyday household contexts.

sentences.text: Baju ini harus diseterika sebelum dipakai.
sentences.en: This shirt must be ironed before being worn.

sentences.text: Kemeja Ayah sudah diseterika tadi pagi.
sentences.en: Dad's shirt was already ironed this morning.

sentences.text: Bajuku belum diseterika oleh Ibu.
sentences.en: My clothes have not been ironed by Mom yet.

note: "Kartu kredit" is a neutral everyday term for credit card; contrast with "kartu debit" (debit card); commonly used at shops, hotels, and restaurants.

sentences.text: Saya bayar dengan kartu kredit.
sentences.en: I pay with a credit card.

sentences.text: Apakah bisa pakai kartu kredit di sini?
sentences.en: Can I use a credit card here?

sentences.text: Saya tidak punya kartu kredit.
sentences.en: I don't have a credit card.

note: "Membuang" is the formal verb form; everyday speech often uses "buang" alone; common in phrases like "buang sampah" (throw away trash); don't confuse with "lempar" (to throw/toss something at a target).

sentences.text: Tolong buang sampah itu ke tong.
sentences.en: Please throw that trash into the bin.

sentences.text: Dia membuang botol plastik di sini.
sentences.en: He throws a plastic bottle here.

sentences.text: Jangan buang makanan yang masih baik.
sentences.en: Don't throw away food that is still good.

note: "Memegang" is the formal/active form of the root word "pegang" (to hold/grip something physically); don't confuse with "menjaga" which means to look after or guard.

sentences.text: Dia memegang tangan ibunya dengan erat.
sentences.en: She is holding her mother's hand tightly.

sentences.text: Tolong pegang tas ini sebentar.
sentences.en: Please hold this bag for a moment.

sentences.text: Anak itu memegang balon merah.
sentences.en: The child is holding a red balloon.

note: "Heran" means surprised/amazed; "mengherankan" means something IS surprising — use "heran" to describe how you feel, and "mengherankan" to describe what causes that feeling.

sentences.text: Harga makanan di sini sangat mengherankan.
sentences.en: The food price here is very surprising.

sentences.text: Saya heran melihat pantai yang indah.
sentences.en: I am surprised seeing the beautiful beach.

sentences.text: Cuaca hari ini sungguh mengherankan.
sentences.en: Today's weather is truly surprising.

note: "Menyeterika" is the formal verb form; in casual speech Indonesians often just say "seterika" as both noun (iron) and verb, e.g. "Aku mau seterika baju."

sentences.text: Ibu menyeterika baju di pagi hari.
sentences.en: Mom irons clothes in the morning.

sentences.text: Aku harus menyeterika seragam sekolah.
sentences.en: I have to iron my school uniform.

sentences.text: Dia menyeterika celana sebelum pergi kerja.
sentences.en: She irons her pants before going to work.

note: "Pakaian setelan" refers to a matching suit (jacket and trousers/skirt); more formal than everyday clothes, often worn to offices or ceremonies in Indonesia.

sentences.text: Dia memakai pakaian setelan ke kantor.
sentences.en: He wears a suit to the office.

sentences.text: Pakaian setelan ini berwarna hitam.
sentences.en: This suit is black.

sentences.text: Saya beli pakaian setelan baru kemarin.
sentences.en: I bought a new suit yesterday.

note: 'Segera' means 'immediately/soon'; used in polite requests or urgent situations; similar to 'cepat' (fast) but focuses on doing something without delay.

sentences.text: Tolong segera hubungi dokter sekarang.
sentences.en: Please immediately contact a doctor now.

sentences.text: Dia segera pergi ke pasar.
sentences.en: She immediately went to the market.

sentences.text: Kami harus segera pulang ke rumah.
sentences.en: We must immediately go home.

note: 'Sialan' is a mild Indonesian swear word similar to 'Damn!' or 'Dammit'; it is informal and impolite, so avoid using it in formal situations; related words include 'sial' meaning 'unlucky' or 'bad luck'.

sentences.text: Sialan, aku lupa bawa dompet!
sentences.en: Damn, I forgot to bring my wallet!

sentences.text: Sialan! Motor aku ban-nya bocor.
sentences.en: Damn! My motorbike has a flat tire.

note: "Membungkus" is the formal verb form; "bungkus" is commonly used in everyday speech, also means a 'packet' or 'parcel' (e.g. food takeaway).

sentences.text: Ibu membungkus nasi dengan daun pisang.
sentences.en: Mom wraps the rice with a banana leaf.

sentences.text: Tolong bungkus kado ulang tahun ini.
sentences.en: Please wrap this birthday gift.

sentences.text: Dia membungkus makanan untuk dibawa pulang.
sentences.en: She wraps the food to take home.

note: 'Ember' means 'bucket'; not to be confused with 'api' (fire) — everyday household word, also used at the beach or farm.

sentences.text: Tolong ambil ember di kamar mandi.
sentences.en: Please get the bucket in the bathroom.

sentences.text: Ibu mengisi ember dengan air bersih.
sentences.en: Mom fills the bucket with clean water.

sentences.text: Ember merah itu ada di dapur.
sentences.en: That red bucket is in the kitchen.

english: turn on/switch on (a light or engine)
note: Use 'menghidupkan' for turning on lights, engines, or electronics; not for people or abstract things; related: 'mematikan' (turn off).

sentences.text: Tolong hidupkan lampu di kamar tidur.
sentences.en: Please turn on the light in the bedroom.

sentences.text: Ayah menghidupkan mesin motor setiap pagi.
sentences.en: Dad turns on the motorbike engine every morning.

sentences.text: Bisa hidupkan AC? Panas sekali.
sentences.en: Can you turn on the AC? It's very hot.

english: to dry something in the sun
note: "Menjemur" is the formal/active form; colloquially shortened to "jemur"; commonly used for drying clothes, rice, or fish under the sun — not to be confused with "mengeringkan" which means drying with heat/appliance.

sentences.text: Ibu menjemur baju di halaman rumah.
sentences.en: Mom dries the clothes in the yard.

sentences.text: Adi jemur handuk di bawah matahari.
sentences.en: Adi dries the towel under the sun.

sentences.text: Nenek menjemur ikan di depan rumah.
sentences.en: Grandma dries fish in front of the house.

note: 'Kertas' means paper in general; commonly confused with 'kartu' (card) — use 'kertas' for plain sheets, related words: 'buku' (book), 'pensil' (pencil).

sentences.text: Saya butuh kertas untuk menulis surat.
sentences.en: I need paper to write a letter.

sentences.text: Tolong ambilkan kertas di atas meja.
sentences.en: Please get the paper on the table.

sentences.text: Anak itu menggambar di kertas putih.
sentences.en: That child is drawing on white paper.

note: 'Kotak' means box or square; also used in 'kotak-kotak' (checkered pattern); don't confuse with 'kardus' (cardboard box specifically).

sentences.text: Ada kotak besar di meja itu.
sentences.en: There is a big box on that table.

sentences.text: Saya menyimpan buku di dalam kotak.
sentences.en: I keep books inside a box.

sentences.text: Tolong buka kotak itu sekarang.
sentences.en: Please open that box now.

note: 'Berkata' means 'to say (that)' and is slightly formal; in casual speech Indonesians often use 'bilang' instead; related words: 'kata' (word/say), 'dikatakan' (is said).

sentences.text: Ibu berkata bahwa makan sudah siap.
sentences.en: Mom says that the food is ready.

sentences.text: Pak guru berkata kelas dimulai sekarang.
sentences.en: The teacher says that class starts now.

sentences.text: Dia berkata harga itu sangat mahal.
sentences.en: She says that the price is very expensive.

note: 'Cinta' means romantic love; use 'sayang' for general affection toward family or friends; 'jatuh cinta' means 'to fall in love'.

sentences.text: Aku cinta kamu selamanya.
sentences.en: I love you forever.

sentences.text: Dia jatuh cinta di Bali.
sentences.en: He fell in love in Bali.

sentences.text: Cinta itu indah sekali.
sentences.en: Love is very beautiful.

note: "Diganggu" is the passive form of "ganggu" (to disturb/bother); often confused with "marah" (angry) — use it when someone is bothered or disturbed by something/someone.

sentences.text: Dia diganggu oleh suara bising itu.
sentences.en: She is upset by that loud noise.

sentences.text: Saya tidak mau diganggu saat belajar.
sentences.en: I don't want to be disturbed while studying.

sentences.text: Kucing itu diganggu oleh anak kecil.
sentences.en: The cat is upset by the small child.

note: 'Kaca' means both 'glass' (material) and 'mirror'; for drinking glass use 'gelas' instead.

sentences.text: Dia melihat wajahnya di kaca.
sentences.en: She looks at her face in the mirror.

sentences.text: Kaca jendela itu sangat bersih.
sentences.en: That window glass is very clean.

sentences.text: Tolong jangan sentuh kaca itu.
sentences.en: Please don't touch that glass.

note: 'Majikan' means employer or boss; more formal than 'bos' (borrowed from English), often used in work/household contexts.

sentences.text: Majikan saya sangat baik dan sabar.
sentences.en: My boss is very kind and patient.

sentences.text: Dia bekerja untuk majikan yang kaya.
sentences.en: She works for a rich boss.

sentences.text: Majikan itu memberi gaji setiap bulan.
sentences.en: That boss gives a salary every month.

note: 'Masukkan' is the imperative/command form; 'memasukkan' is the active verb form meaning to put something into a container or place.

sentences.text: Tolong masukkan baju ke dalam tas.
sentences.en: Please put the clothes into the bag.

sentences.text: Ibu memasukkan sayur ke dalam panci.
sentences.en: Mom puts vegetables into the pot.

sentences.text: Masukkan uang ke dalam dompet kamu.
sentences.en: Put the money into your wallet.

note: 'Rendah' means low or short in height/level; opposite is 'tinggi'; used for prices, volume, buildings, and more.

sentences.text: Harga buah itu sangat rendah hari ini.
sentences.en: The price of that fruit is very low today.

sentences.text: Tolong kecilkan volume musik yang rendah.
sentences.en: Please turn down the low music volume.

sentences.text: Atap rumah itu sangat rendah.
sentences.en: The roof of that house is very low.

english: to be aware, to be conscious
note: 'Sadar' means to be aware or conscious; commonly used in phrases like 'sadar diri' (self-aware); do not confuse with 'tahu' (to know a fact).

sentences.text: Dia tidak sadar ada orang di sana.
sentences.en: He is not aware there is someone there.

sentences.text: Saya sadar kita harus jaga kebersihan pantai.
sentences.en: I am aware we must keep the beach clean.

sentences.text: Anak itu sadar setelah minum air.
sentences.en: The child became conscious after drinking water.

note: 'Saku' means pocket (on clothing); not to be confused with 'kantong' which can also mean pocket or bag in some regions; commonly used in everyday speech.

sentences.text: Kunci ada di dalam saku saya.
sentences.en: The key is in my pocket.

sentences.text: Saku celana saya kecil sekali.
sentences.en: My pants pocket is very small.

sentences.text: Dia menyimpan uang di saku baju.
sentences.en: He keeps money in his shirt pocket.

note: 'Sesuatu' means 'something' (an unspecified thing); used in everyday speech across all registers; related words: 'seseorang' (someone), 'suatu' (a certain).

sentences.text: Saya ingin makan sesuatu yang enak.
sentences.en: I want to eat something delicious.

sentences.text: Ada sesuatu di dalam tas kamu.
sentences.en: There is something inside your bag.

sentences.text: Dia membeli sesuatu di pasar hari ini.
sentences.en: She bought something at the market today.

note: 'Sisir' means a comb (noun); also used as a verb meaning to comb — common in daily grooming contexts.

sentences.text: Saya mencari sisir di kamar mandi.
sentences.en: I am looking for a comb in the bathroom.

sentences.text: Adik memakai sisir setiap pagi.
sentences.en: My younger sibling uses a comb every morning.

sentences.text: Di mana sisir saya?
sentences.en: Where is my comb?

note: "Menambah" is the formal/active form of "tambah" (to add); commonly used in everyday speech; related words include "tambahan" (addition/extra) and "bertambah" (to increase/grow).

sentences.text: Saya menambah gula ke dalam kopi.
sentences.en: I add sugar to the coffee.

sentences.text: Ibu menambah sayur ke dalam sup.
sentences.en: Mom adds vegetables to the soup.

sentences.text: Dia menambah uang untuk beli nasi.
sentences.en: He adds money to buy rice.

note: 'Demikian' means 'thus/so/like that'; used in slightly formal speech; related to 'begitu' (more casual) and often seen in closing statements like 'demikian informasi ini'.

sentences.text: Demikian cerita tentang liburan saya.
sentences.en: Thus is the story about my holiday.

sentences.text: Guru berkata demikian kepada murid.
sentences.en: The teacher said so to the students.

sentences.text: Demikian pengumuman dari kepala sekolah.
sentences.en: Thus is the announcement from the principal.

note: 'Perbedaan' means 'difference'; related to 'beda' (different); used in formal and everyday speech to compare two things.

sentences.text: Apa perbedaan antara kopi dan teh?
sentences.en: What is the difference between coffee and tea?

sentences.text: Saya melihat perbedaan harga di pasar.
sentences.en: I see a difference in prices at the market.

sentences.text: Tidak ada perbedaan besar di sini.
sentences.en: There is no big difference here.

english: actually, as a matter of fact
note: "Sebenarnya" is neutral-register and used to clarify or correct something; similar to "sebetulnya" (slightly more formal/colloquial overlap); place it at the start or before the clarified idea.

sentences.text: Sebenarnya saya tidak suka kopi.
sentences.en: Actually, I don't like coffee.

sentences.text: Dia sebenarnya orang Bali, bukan Jawa.
sentences.en: He is actually from Bali, not Java.

sentences.text: Sebenarnya harga ini sudah murah.
sentences.en: Actually, this price is already cheap.

note: 'Sehingga' means 'so that' or 'so' (result); used in slightly formal writing, beginners may confuse it with 'supaya' (in order to/so that = purpose).

sentences.text: Dia belajar keras sehingga lulus ujian.
sentences.en: She studies hard so that she passes the exam.

sentences.text: Hujan turun sehingga jalan menjadi basah.
sentences.en: Rain fell so that the road became wet.

sentences.text: Saya makan banyak sehingga kenyang sekarang.
sentences.en: I ate a lot so that I am full now.

note: 'Tanpa' means 'without' and is used before nouns or verbs; it does not change form and is more formal than dropping the word entirely in casual speech.

sentences.text: Saya minum kopi tanpa gula setiap pagi.
sentences.en: I drink coffee without sugar every morning.

sentences.text: Dia pergi tanpa membawa uang.
sentences.en: He left without bringing money.

sentences.text: Kami makan nasi tanpa lauk hari ini.
sentences.en: We ate rice without side dishes today.

note: 'Terkejut' means surprised or startled; related words include 'kaget' (more informal/sudden fright) and 'heran' (amazed/puzzled).

sentences.text: Saya terkejut melihat hadiah di meja.
sentences.en: I was surprised to see a gift on the table.

sentences.text: Dia terkejut karena anjing itu menggonggong.
sentences.en: She was startled because the dog barked.

sentences.text: Kami terkejut saat hujan turun tiba-tiba.
sentences.en: We were surprised when the rain suddenly fell.

note: "Tersenyum" means "to smile" and is an intransitive verb; use "senyum" as the noun form (e.g., senyumnya indah = her smile is beautiful).

sentences.text: Dia tersenyum ketika melihat temannya.
sentences.en: She smiles when she sees her friend.

sentences.text: Bayi itu tersenyum kepada ibunya.
sentences.en: The baby smiles at his mother.

sentences.text: Saya tersenyum saat makan nasi goreng.
sentences.en: I smile when eating fried rice.

note: "Menunjukkan" is the formal/written form; "tunjukkan" is the imperative/spoken shortcut — both mean 'to show'; often confused with "memperlihatkan" (to display/reveal).

sentences.text: Tolong tunjukkan peta itu kepada saya.
sentences.en: Please show that map to me.

sentences.text: Dia menunjukkan jalan ke pantai.
sentences.en: He/She shows the way to the beach.

sentences.text: Tunjukkan kartu identitas kamu di sini.
sentences.en: Show your ID card here.

note: 'Memisahkan' is the formal/active form; 'pisahkan' is the imperative (command) form — both mean 'to separate'; commonly used when sorting items or dividing things apart.

sentences.text: Tolong pisahkan sampah plastik dan kertas.
sentences.en: Please separate the plastic and paper trash.

sentences.text: Ibu memisahkan baju bersih dan baju kotor.
sentences.en: Mom separates the clean clothes and dirty clothes.

sentences.text: Guru memisahkan dua anak yang berkelahi.
sentences.en: The teacher separates the two children who are fighting.

note: 'Untung' means 'luckily/fortunately'; also means 'profit' in business contexts — don't confuse them.

sentences.text: Untung saya membawa payung hari ini.
sentences.en: Luckily I brought an umbrella today.

sentences.text: Untung warung itu masih buka sekarang.
sentences.en: Luckily that food stall is still open now.

sentences.text: Untung ada taksi di sini.
sentences.en: Luckily there is a taxi here.

note: 'Begini' means 'like this' or 'this way'; it often introduces an explanation or demonstrates something, and is commonly confused with 'begitu' (like that/that way).

sentences.text: Caranya begini, ikuti langkah-langkah saya.
sentences.en: The way is like this, follow my steps.

sentences.text: Begini cara membuat nasi goreng.
sentences.en: This is how to make fried rice.

sentences.text: Maaf, situasinya begini sekarang.
sentences.en: Sorry, the situation is like this now.

note: "Dikurangi" is the passive form of "kurangi" (reduce/subtract); commonly used in math, prices, and portions; related words: "berkurang" (to decrease), "pengurangan" (reduction).

sentences.text: Harga tiket ini dikurangi sepuluh persen.
sentences.en: The price of this ticket is reduced by ten percent.

sentences.text: Nasinya dikurangi karena saya sedang diet.
sentences.en: The rice portion is reduced because I am on a diet.

sentences.text: Sepuluh dikurangi tiga sama dengan tujuh.
sentences.en: Ten minus three equals seven.

note: 'Harga mati' literally means 'fixed/dead price', used when a seller refuses to negotiate further; also means 'non-negotiable final price' in markets.

sentences.text: Ini harga mati, tidak bisa kurang.
sentences.en: This is the lowest price, it cannot be less.

sentences.text: Pedagang itu bilang harga mati.
sentences.en: That seller said it is the final price.

sentences.text: Harga mati di sini lima puluh ribu.
sentences.en: The lowest price here is fifty thousand.

note: 'Harga pas' means a fixed/set price with no bargaining; common in modern shops vs. traditional markets where haggling ('tawar-menawar') is expected.

sentences.text: Toko ini menjual dengan harga pas.
sentences.en: This shop sells at a fixed price.

sentences.text: Di sini harga pas, tidak bisa tawar.
sentences.en: Here the price is fixed, you cannot bargain.

sentences.text: Berapa harga pas kaos ini?
sentences.en: What is the fixed price of this t-shirt?

note: 'Lain kali' means 'next time' or 'some other time'; common in casual speech to politely postpone plans; related: 'nanti' (later), 'besok' (tomorrow).

sentences.text: Lain kali kita makan bersama, ya?
sentences.en: Some other time we eat together, okay?

sentences.text: Maaf, lain kali saja aku datang.
sentences.en: Sorry, I will come some other time.

sentences.text: Oke, lain kali kita pergi ke pantai.
sentences.en: Okay, next time we go to the beach.

note: 'ndak' is an informal/spoken shortening of 'tidak' (not/no), common in casual everyday speech; similar informal forms include 'nggak' and 'tak'.

sentences.text: Saya ndak mau makan nasi goreng.
sentences.en: I don't want to eat fried rice.

sentences.text: Dia ndak ada di rumah sekarang.
sentences.en: He/She is not at home right now.

sentences.text: Ndak apa-apa, besok kita coba lagi.
sentences.en: It's okay, tomorrow we'll try again.

note: 'Pikir-pikir' is informal/colloquial for 'to think it over'; often used alone or with 'dulu' (first) as 'pikir-pikir dulu' meaning 'let me think about it first'

sentences.text: Saya mau pikir-pikir dulu sebelum memutuskan.
sentences.en: I want to think it over first before deciding.

sentences.text: Dia pikir-pikir soal kerja baru itu.
sentences.en: She is considering that new job.

sentences.text: Kami pikir-pikir dulu sebelum beli oleh-oleh.
sentences.en: We think it over first before buying souvenirs.

note: "Tawar" means to bargain/negotiate price; common in markets; related: "menawar" (to make an offer), "harga" (price)

sentences.text: Saya suka tawar di pasar tradisional.
sentences.en: I like bargaining at the traditional market.

sentences.text: Boleh saya tawar harga ini?
sentences.en: May I bargain on this price?

sentences.text: Di Bali, tawar adalah hal biasa.
sentences.en: In Bali, bargaining is a normal thing.

note: "Tawar-menawar" is an informal, everyday phrase for bargaining over price, common at markets; related to "menawar" (to make an offer).

sentences.text: Saya suka tawar-menawar di pasar.
sentences.en: I like to bargain at the market.

sentences.text: Mereka tawar-menawar harga baju itu.
sentences.en: They are negotiating the price of that shirt.

sentences.text: Boleh kita tawar-menawar di sini?
sentences.en: Can we bargain here?

note: "Menawarkan" is the formal/written form; "tawarkan" is the imperative or colloquial form; use it when presenting or suggesting something to someone, not to be confused with "memberikan" (to give).

sentences.text: Dia menawarkan kopi kepada tamu.
sentences.en: She offers coffee to the guest.

sentences.text: Pedagang itu menawarkan buah segar.
sentences.en: That seller offers fresh fruit.

sentences.text: Tawarkan kursi kepada nenek itu.
sentences.en: Offer a seat to that grandmother.

note: 'Bentuk' means 'form' or 'shape'; commonly used in art, school, and descriptions; related to 'berbentuk' (shaped like) and 'membentuk' (to form/create).

sentences.text: Apa bentuk bangunan itu?
sentences.en: What is the shape of that building?

sentences.text: Kue ini bentuk bintang yang lucu.
sentences.en: This cake is in the shape of a cute star.

sentences.text: Anak itu belajar bentuk lingkaran di sekolah.
sentences.en: That child is learning the circle shape at school.

note: 'Beranda' means a verandah or front porch; common in Indonesian homes; also informally used for a homepage/feed on apps.

sentences.text: Kami duduk di beranda rumah kami.
sentences.en: We sit on the verandah of our house.

sentences.text: Ibu minum teh di beranda pagi ini.
sentences.en: Mom drinks tea on the verandah this morning.

sentences.text: Ada kursi di beranda itu.
sentences.en: There is a chair on that verandah.

english: a roof tile, tiles (for a roof)
note: 'Genteng' refers to a clay or ceramic roof tile; commonly used in everyday speech about house construction or repairs, distinct from 'atap' which means roof in general.

sentences.text: Genteng rumah kami pecah karena hujan deras.
sentences.en: Our roof tile cracked because of the heavy rain.

sentences.text: Ayah membeli genteng baru untuk rumah kita.
sentences.en: Dad bought new roof tiles for our house.

sentences.text: Tukang itu memasang genteng dengan hati-hati.
sentences.en: The worker installed the roof tiles carefully.

note: 'Seng' refers to corrugated iron/zinc roofing sheets, very common in Indonesian villages; not to be confused with 'seng' meaning 'zinc' in chemistry contexts.

sentences.text: Atap rumah kami terbuat dari seng.
sentences.en: The roof of our house is made of corrugated iron.

sentences.text: Seng itu bocor saat hujan deras.
sentences.en: The corrugated iron leaks when it rains heavily.

sentences.text: Pak Budi membeli seng baru kemarin.
sentences.en: Mr. Budi bought new corrugated iron yesterday.

note: "Suara" means both 'voice' and 'sound/noise'; also used for 'vote' in formal contexts. Do not confuse with "bunyi" (a more general sound/noise).

sentences.text: Suara guru itu sangat keras.
sentences.en: The teacher's voice is very loud.

sentences.text: Saya mendengar suara burung di luar.
sentences.en: I hear the sound of birds outside.

sentences.text: Suara musik itu sangat indah.
sentences.en: The sound of that music is very beautiful.

note: "Apa lagi?" means "what else?" and is used to ask if there is anything more; very common in shops and casual conversation.

sentences.text: Mau pesan apa lagi, Pak?
sentences.en: What else would you like to order, Sir?

sentences.text: Ada apa lagi di menu ini?
sentences.en: What else is on this menu?

sentences.text: Kamu mau beli apa lagi?
sentences.en: What else do you want to buy?

english: a tub (in a bathroom), the tray (on the back of a truck)
note: "Bak" is an everyday informal word; "bak mandi" means bathroom tub/water tub, while "bak truk" means the open tray/bed of a truck.

sentences.text: Tolong isi bak mandi dengan air.
sentences.en: Please fill the bathroom tub with water.

sentences.text: Ayah menaruh barang di bak truk.
sentences.en: Father put the goods in the truck tray.

note: 'Bergengsi' means prestigious/high-status; used for schools, jobs, or events; related: 'gengsi' (status/pride), slightly formal but common in everyday speech

sentences.text: Universitas itu sangat bergengsi di Indonesia.
sentences.en: That university is very prestigious in Indonesia.

sentences.text: Dia bekerja di perusahaan bergengsi.
sentences.en: He works at a prestigious company.

sentences.text: Festival ini adalah acara bergengsi di Bali.
sentences.en: This festival is a prestigious event in Bali.

note: "Menggabungkan" is the formal verb form; "gabungkan" is the imperative/command form — both mean 'to combine/merge'; often used when mixing ingredients, joining groups, or merging files.

sentences.text: Dia menggabungkan sayur dan buah di piring.
sentences.en: She combines vegetables and fruit on the plate.

sentences.text: Tolong gabungkan dua kelompok ini menjadi satu.
sentences.en: Please merge these two groups into one.

sentences.text: Ibu menggabungkan tepung dan gula untuk kue.
sentences.en: Mom combines flour and sugar for the cake.

english: an alley, a passageway, a corridor
note: "Gang" means a narrow alley or small passageway between buildings; very common in Indonesian neighborhoods (kampung); not to be confused with English "gang" (criminal group).

sentences.text: Rumah saya ada di gang kecil.
sentences.en: My house is in a small alley.

sentences.text: Gang ini sempit dan gelap.
sentences.en: This alley is narrow and dark.

sentences.text: Anak-anak bermain di gang depan.
sentences.en: The children are playing in the alley out front.

english: to make a contact with someone
note: "Menghubungi" is the formal/full form; "hubungi" is the imperative or informal root, often used in signs like "Hubungi kami" (Contact us); not to be confused with "bertemu" (to meet in person).

sentences.text: Saya akan menghubungi dokter besok pagi.
sentences.en: I will contact the doctor tomorrow morning.

sentences.text: Tolong hubungi saya jika ada masalah.
sentences.en: Please contact me if there is a problem.

sentences.text: Dia lupa menghubungi teman-temannya.
sentences.en: He forgot to contact his friends.

english: one traditional style of Javanese roof
note: "Joglo" refers to a traditional Javanese roof style with a tall, tiered peak; commonly seen on Javanese houses and cultural buildings; related words include "rumah adat" (traditional house) and "pendopo" (open pavilion).

sentences.text: Rumah ini memakai atap joglo yang indah.
sentences.en: This house uses a beautiful joglo roof.

sentences.text: Atap joglo adalah atap tradisional Jawa.
sentences.en: The joglo roof is a traditional Javanese roof.

sentences.text: Saya suka desain joglo di museum itu.
sentences.en: I like the joglo design at that museum.

note: 'Kagum' is a common, neutral adjective/verb meaning amazed or full of admiration; often paired with 'merasa' (to feel) or 'sangat' (very); related word: 'kekaguman' (admiration, noun).

sentences.text: Saya kagum melihat pantai yang indah.
sentences.en: I am amazed seeing the beautiful beach.

sentences.text: Dia sangat kagum dengan tari Bali.
sentences.en: She is very amazed by Balinese dance.

sentences.text: Kami kagum melihat upacara itu.
sentences.en: We are amazed watching that ceremony.

note: 'Kebun Raya' specifically refers to the famous Bogor Botanical Garden; 'kebun' means garden/yard, 'raya' means grand/great — often used as a proper noun.

sentences.text: Kami pergi ke Kebun Raya hari ini.
sentences.en: We are going to the Botanical Garden today.

sentences.text: Kebun Raya sangat indah dan hijau.
sentences.en: The Botanical Garden is very beautiful and green.

sentences.text: Banyak pohon besar di Kebun Raya.
sentences.en: There are many big trees in the Botanical Garden.

note: 'Kredit' means a bank loan or buying on installment; commonly used in 'kredit motor' (motorcycle loan) or 'kartu kredit' (credit card).

sentences.text: Dia beli motor dengan kredit dari bank.
sentences.en: He bought a motorcycle with a loan from the bank.

sentences.text: Saya bayar kredit setiap bulan.
sentences.en: I pay the loan installment every month.

sentences.text: Apakah kamu punya kartu kredit?
sentences.en: Do you have a credit card?

note: 'Kulkas' is the everyday informal word for refrigerator in Indonesian, borrowed from Dutch 'koelkast'; also sometimes called 'lemari es' in more formal contexts.

sentences.text: Tolong taruh susu itu di dalam kulkas.
sentences.en: Please put that milk inside the refrigerator.

sentences.text: Kulkas di dapur saya sangat besar.
sentences.en: The refrigerator in my kitchen is very big.

sentences.text: Air di kulkas sangat dingin dan segar.
sentences.en: The water in the refrigerator is very cold and refreshing.

english: advanced (talking about something that occurs at a further stage)
note: "Lanjut" means to continue or move to a next/further stage; often used in casual speech to say 'let's continue' or describe an advanced level, not to be confused with "lanjutan" (continuation/follow-up).

sentences.text: Kelas lanjut dimulai besok pagi.
sentences.en: The advanced class starts tomorrow morning.

sentences.text: Dia ikut kursus lanjut di Bali.
sentences.en: She is taking an advanced course in Bali.

sentences.text: Setelah istirahat, kita lanjut belajar.
sentences.en: After the break, we continue studying.

note: 'Lokasi' is a neutral everyday word for location or site; commonly used when asking for directions or describing a place; related words include 'tempat' (place) and 'alamat' (address).

sentences.text: Di mana lokasi hotel ini?
sentences.en: Where is the location of this hotel?

sentences.text: Lokasi pantai itu sangat indah.
sentences.en: The location of that beach is very beautiful.

sentences.text: Saya tidak tahu lokasi restoran itu.
sentences.en: I don't know the location of that restaurant.

note: "Masa kini" means 'the present time / nowadays'; often used in contrast with 'masa lalu' (the past) or 'masa depan' (the future).

sentences.text: Teknologi masa kini sangat canggih dan cepat.
sentences.en: Technology nowadays is very advanced and fast.

sentences.text: Anak muda masa kini suka pakai media sosial.
sentences.en: Young people nowadays like to use social media.

note: "Masa lampau" means 'the past' and is used in formal or written contexts; in casual speech Indonesians often say "dulu" instead; related words include "masa depan" (the future) and "masa kini" (the present).

sentences.text: Saya suka belajar tentang masa lampau.
sentences.en: I like learning about the past.

sentences.text: Masa lampau Bali sangat menarik.
sentences.en: Bali's past is very interesting.

note: 'Memiliki' is formal; everyday speech often uses 'punya' instead; 'miliki' is the base form used in commands or compounds.

sentences.text: Saya memiliki satu kucing di rumah.
sentences.en: I have one cat at home.

sentences.text: Dia memiliki sepeda baru yang bagus.
sentences.en: He has a nice new bicycle.

note: 'Mesin cuci piring' literally means 'dish-washing machine'; less common in everyday Indonesian homes than hand-washing, but found in restaurants and modern kitchens; not to be confused with 'mesin cuci' (washing machine for clothes).

sentences.text: Restoran itu punya mesin cuci piring besar.
sentences.en: That restaurant has a big dishwasher.

sentences.text: Ibu membeli mesin cuci piring baru.
sentences.en: Mom bought a new dishwasher.

sentences.text: Mesin cuci piring ini sangat praktis.
sentences.en: This dishwasher is very practical.

note: 'Mutiara' means pearl; commonly seen in jewelry contexts; related words: 'kalung mutiara' (pearl necklace), 'cincin mutiara' (pearl ring).

sentences.text: Ibu membeli kalung mutiara di pasar.
sentences.en: Mom bought a pearl necklace at the market.

sentences.text: Mutiara ini sangat indah dan mahal.
sentences.en: This pearl is very beautiful and expensive.

sentences.text: Saya suka cincin mutiara milik nenek.
sentences.en: I like grandmother's pearl ring.

note: "Nyaman" means comfortable or pleasant, often describing a place or environment; don't confuse with "senang" (happy) or "enak" (tasty/comfortable for feelings).

sentences.text: Kamar hotel ini sangat nyaman.
sentences.en: This hotel room is very pleasant.

sentences.text: Taman ini nyaman untuk duduk santai.
sentences.en: This park is pleasant for sitting and relaxing.

sentences.text: Saya suka kafe yang nyaman ini.
sentences.en: I like this pleasant café.

english: a reception area in a traditional Javanese house
note: "Pendopo" refers to an open-sided pavilion or reception hall in a traditional Javanese home or official building; often confused with a simple porch, but it is a formal gathering space.

sentences.text: Tamu duduk di pendopo rumah kami.
sentences.en: The guests sit in the reception pavilion of our house.

sentences.text: Pendopo itu besar dan indah.
sentences.en: That reception pavilion is big and beautiful.

sentences.text: Kami bertemu di pendopo desa.
sentences.en: We meet at the village reception pavilion.

note: 'Peralatan' is a neutral everyday noun meaning 'equipment/tools/supplies'; commonly used with 'masak' (cooking), 'tulis' (writing), or 'kerja' (work); related word: 'alat' (a single tool).

sentences.text: Saya membeli peralatan masak di pasar.
sentences.en: I buy cooking equipment at the market.

sentences.text: Peralatan sekolah adik ada di tas.
sentences.en: My younger sibling's school supplies are in the bag.

sentences.text: Kami perlu peralatan untuk berkemah besok.
sentences.en: We need equipment for camping tomorrow.

note: 'Perumahan' refers to a planned residential housing complex or estate; not to be confused with 'rumah' (a single house) or 'apartemen' (apartment building).

sentences.text: Saya tinggal di perumahan baru itu.
sentences.en: I live in that new housing complex.

sentences.text: Perumahan ini dekat dengan sekolah.
sentences.en: This housing complex is close to the school.

sentences.text: Ada taman di dalam perumahan kami.
sentences.en: There is a park inside our housing complex.

note: 'Sejuk' means cool/refreshing (pleasant temperature); don't confuse with 'dingin' (cold/unfriendly) — 'sejuk' is always positive and comfortable.

sentences.text: Udara di pegunungan sangat sejuk.
sentences.en: The air in the mountains is very cool.

sentences.text: Ruangan ini sejuk karena ada AC.
sentences.en: This room is cool because there is AC.

sentences.text: Angin pantai terasa sejuk dan segar.
sentences.en: The beach breeze feels cool and fresh.

note: 'Tempat tinggal' is a neutral, formal-ish term for where someone lives; everyday speech also uses 'rumah' (house) or 'alamat' (address).

sentences.text: Di mana tempat tinggal kamu sekarang?
sentences.en: Where do you live now?

sentences.text: Tempat tinggal saya dekat pantai.
sentences.en: My place of residence is near the beach.

sentences.text: Dia mencari tempat tinggal yang murah.
sentences.en: He is looking for a cheap place to live.

note: 'Wastafel' is a common loanword (from Dutch) used in everyday Indonesian for a bathroom or kitchen sink/washbasin; beginners may confuse it with 'bak mandi' (bathtub/bath basin).

sentences.text: Ada wastafel di kamar mandi kami.
sentences.en: There is a washbasin in our bathroom.

sentences.text: Saya cuci tangan di wastafel.
sentences.en: I wash my hands at the washbasin.

sentences.text: Wastafel itu kotor sekali.
sentences.en: That washbasin is very dirty.

note: 'Membutuhkan' is the formal/written form; 'butuh' alone is more casual in speech; often confused with 'mau' (want) — 'butuh' means genuine need, not just desire.

sentences.text: Saya membutuhkan air setelah berolahraga.
sentences.en: I need water after exercising.

sentences.text: Dia membutuhkan bantuan di dapur.
sentences.en: She needs help in the kitchen.

sentences.text: Kami butuhkan waktu untuk istirahat.
sentences.en: We need time to rest.

english: a loan of money, a lend of something
note: 'Pinjaman' is the noun form of 'meminjam' (to borrow); used for money loans or borrowed items; not to be confused with 'hutang' (debt).

sentences.text: Saya mengajukan pinjaman ke bank hari ini.
sentences.en: I applied for a loan at the bank today.

sentences.text: Pinjaman itu harus dibayar bulan depan.
sentences.en: The loan must be paid back next month.

sentences.text: Dia mendapat pinjaman dari temannya.
sentences.en: He got a loan from his friend.
